content: The SBDS protein, also known as the ribosome maturation protein SBDS, is encoded by the SBDS gene in humans. While an alternative transcript of this gene has been identified, its biological significance remains unclear. This gene is closely associated with a pseudogene located distally. The SBDS gene encodes a member of a highly conserved protein family that is present across a wide range of species, including archaea, vertebrates, and plants. Function of SBDS Protein The SBDS protein is believed to play a role in RNA metabolism, although its precise function has not been fully determined. It appears to be critical for ribosome function or assembly. Experimental knockdown of SBDS expression has been shown to increase apoptosis in differentiating erythroid cells, likely due to elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS). This indicates that SBDS is essential for normal erythropoiesis. The protein family to which SBDS belongs is highly conserved across species, including archaea, vertebrates, and plants. Members of this family, including SBDS proteins in humans and mice, are implicated in RNA metabolism. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), an autosomal recessive disorder, is associated with mutations in the SBDS gene. Clinical manifestations of SDS include pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, hematological abnormalities, and skeletal defects. Several uncharacterized hydrophilic proteins, approximately 30 kDa in size, share regions of similarity with SBDS. These include: Mouse protein 22A3 Hypothetical protein YLR022c from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (chromosome XII) Hypothetical protein W06E11.4 from Caenorhabditis elegans Hypothetical protein MJ0592 from Methanococcus jannaschii The SBDS protein sequence is highly conserved across species, from archaea to vertebrates and plants. Structure of SBDS Protein The SBDS protein consists of three distinct domains: 1. N-terminal conserved FYSH domain 2. Central helical domain 3. C-terminal domain containing an RNA-binding motif N-terminal Domain Function: The N-terminal domain is of critical importance, as mutations in this region are frequently associated with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. This domain shares distant structural and sequence homology with the yeast protein YHR087W, which is involved in RNA metabolism. It is therefore likely that the SBDS N-terminal domain also plays a role in RNA metabolism. Structure: The N-terminal domain exhibits a novel mixed alpha-beta fold, consisting of four beta-strands and four alpha-helices arranged in a three-stranded anti-parallel beta-sheet. Central Domain Function: The function of the central domain remains unclear. It may be involved in binding to DNA or RNA, or in forming protein-protein complexes. However, its specific role is difficult to infer due to the structural similarity of this domain to proteins found in archaea. Structure: The central domain contains a winged helix-turn-helix structure, which is a common structural motif. C-terminal Domain Function: The C-terminal domain is highly conserved across species, from archaea to vertebrates and plants. It is thought to play a role in RNA metabolism, but its precise function has not yet been determined. The structural characteristics of this domain make it challenging to predict its specific role. Structure: The C-terminal domain adopts a ferredoxin-like fold, characterized by a four-stranded beta-sheet with two helices on one side. Clinical Significance Mutations in the SBDS gene are associated with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. The two most common mutations linked to this syndrome are: 1. A substitution at positions 183–184 (TA→CT), resulting in a premature stop codon (K62X). 2. A frameshift mutation at position 258 (2T→C), leading to a stop codon (C84fsX3).
